statement: Counterparty credit exposure cannot be netted across counterparties, so it must be calculated at the netting-set level for thousands of counterparties and over many future holding periods, which greatly increases computational intensity.
explanation: Unlike market risk VaR, where gains on one position offset losses on another, exposure cannot be netted across counterparties. Each netting set must be simulated over many future holding periods, so the computation is very intensive.
originalText: Exposure cannot be netted across counterparties, so it must be calculated at the netting‑set level for thousands of counterparties and over many future holding periods, greatly increasing computational intensity.

statement: Counterparty credit exposure is measured over a single short holding period.
explanation: Market risk VaR uses a short holding period, but counterparty exposure must be simulated over multiple, long future holding periods (years or even decades).
originalText: Counterparty exposure is measured over a single short holding period, which is too short for derivatives.
correction: Counterparty credit exposure is measured over multiple long future holding periods.

statement: The long holding period of balance sheet assets and liabilities is one of the main challenges in calculating economic capital for interest rate risk in the banking book.
explanation: Banking-book positions are held for a long time and their cash flows are uncertain because of embedded optionality such as prepayment and non-maturity deposits. Together these make the capital computation difficult.
originalText: The long holding period of balance sheet assets and liabilities.

statement: Copulas are more flexible than a covariance matrix and allow for nonlinearities and higher-order dependencies.
explanation: A copula joins the marginal distributions into a joint distribution with flexible functional forms, so it relaxes the linear-correlation limitation of the covariance matrix. Its drawbacks are that the parameterization is hard to validate and the joint distribution is hard to build.
originalText: Is more flexible than a covariance matrix and allows for nonlinearities and higher‑order dependencies.

statement: With fixed (constant) diversification, the diversification effect is sensitive to the underlying interactions between the different risk components.
explanation: Constant diversification simply subtracts a fixed percentage from the sum of the risks, so it is insensitive to the underlying interactions between risk types.
originalText: The effect of fixed diversification is sensitive to underlying interactions between the different components.
correction: With fixed (constant) diversification, the diversification effect is insensitive to the underlying interactions between the different risk components.

statement: The variance-covariance matrix approach to risk aggregation makes inter-risk correlations easy to estimate.
explanation: Under the variance-covariance approach the correlations between risk types are difficult to estimate, and the linear structure also misses nonlinearities in the dependence.
originalText: The method is easy to use as it easily estimates inter‑risk correlations and does not capture nonlinearities.
correction: The variance-covariance matrix approach to risk aggregation makes inter-risk correlations difficult to estimate.

statement: Complex simulation is one of the characteristics of the unit of account used in risk aggregation.
explanation: The unit of account is defined by three characteristics: the risk metric, the confidence level and the time horizon. Simulation is a method for combining risks, not a characteristic of the common risk currency.
originalText: Complex simulation

statement: The risk metric is one of the characteristics of the unit of account used in risk aggregation.
explanation: The unit of account puts different risk types into comparable units and is defined by the risk metric, the confidence level and the time horizon.
originalText: Risk metric

statement: The time horizon is one of the characteristics of the unit of account used in risk aggregation.
explanation: The unit of account is defined by the risk metric, the confidence level and the time horizon, so that risks of different types can be expressed in a common currency.
originalText: Time horizon

statement: Precision is one of the desirable characteristics of a risk measure listed by the BIS for use in an economic capital framework.
explanation: The BIS list covers qualities such as being intuitive, stable, easy to compute, easy to understand, coherent and interpretable in economic terms. Precision is not on the list, because no measure is perfect and estimates depend on model assumptions.
originalText: Precise

statement: Coherence is a desirable characteristic of a risk measure within the economic capital framework.
explanation: A coherent risk measure satisfies monotonicity, positive homogeneity, translation invariance and subadditivity, and coherence is one of the characteristics the BIS lists as desirable.
originalText: Coherent

statement: Being easy to compute is a desirable characteristic of a risk measure within the economic capital framework.
explanation: Ease of computation is on the BIS list of desirable characteristics, and a more complex measure needs evidence that its added accuracy outweighs its added complexity.
originalText: Easy to compute

statement: Standard deviation is not a coherent risk measure because it violates the monotonicity condition.
explanation: Standard deviation treats upside and downside dispersion alike, so it can rank a portfolio that always pays at least as much as another as the riskier one. This violates monotonicity, and it is also not stable.
originalText: It is not coherent because it violates the monotonicity condition

statement: Standard deviation is not an intuitive risk measure.
explanation: Standard deviation is sufficiently intuitive and easy to understand. The measures that lack intuition are the spectral and distorted risk measures.
originalText: It is not intuitive
correction: Standard deviation is an intuitive risk measure.

statement: Standard deviation is not easy to compute.
explanation: Standard deviation is easy to compute because it needs only an estimate of the loss distribution. Its weaknesses are instability and lack of coherence.
originalText: It is not easy to compute
correction: Standard deviation is easy to compute.

statement: VaR is not stable because it depends on assumptions about the loss distribution.
explanation: VaR is a single quantile estimate, so small changes in distributional assumptions or in simulation runs can move it materially. Apart from its lack of coherence, this instability is its main weakness as an economic capital measure.
originalText: It is not stable because it depends on assumptions about the loss distribution

statement: VaR is not an intuitive risk measure.
explanation: VaR is rated as intuitive, sufficiently easy to compute and easy to understand, and it is easier to communicate to senior management than expected shortfall.
originalText: It is not intuitive
correction: VaR is an intuitive risk measure.

statement: Expected shortfall does not lend itself to easy interpretation and has no clear link to the bank's desired target rating.
explanation: Expected shortfall averages losses over the whole tail, which is harder to interpret and does not map directly to a confidence level tied to a target rating, unlike VaR.
originalText: It does not lend itself to easy interpretation and has no clear link to the bank’s desired target rating

statement: Expected shortfall is not coherent because it violates subadditivity.
explanation: It is VaR that can violate subadditivity. Expected shortfall is a coherent risk measure.
originalText: It is not coherent because it violates subadditivity
correction: Expected shortfall is coherent because it satisfies subadditivity.

changes.from: is not coherent because it violates

statement: Expected shortfall cannot be decomposed into the contributions of business lines.
explanation: Expected shortfall can be decomposed consistently with the portfolio measure and is increasingly used for capital allocation.
originalText: It cannot be decomposed into contributions of business lines
correction: Expected shortfall can be decomposed into the contributions of business lines.

statement: Spectral and distorted risk measures are not intuitive.
explanation: Using them requires choosing a spectrum or distortion function that has no natural intuitive interpretation. This lack of intuition is a weakness, and these measures are rarely used in practice.
originalText: They are not intuitive

statement: Spectral and distorted risk measures are not coherent.
explanation: Spectral and distorted risk measures are coherent. Their weakness is that they are not intuitive.
originalText: They are not coherent
correction: Spectral and distorted risk measures are coherent.

statement: Spectral and distorted risk measures are not easy to compute.
explanation: They are sufficiently easy to compute, since the loss distribution is simply weighted by the spectrum or distortion function.
originalText: They are not easy to compute
correction: Spectral and distorted risk measures are sufficiently easy to compute.

statement: The perspective of creditors, rating agencies and supervisors is likely to lead to the highest confidence level in calibrating economic capital.
explanation: These external stakeholders want capital that minimises the risk of bankruptcy, so they favour very high confidence levels. Management uses lower confidence levels for capital allocation and for identifying exposures critical to profit.
originalText: Perspective of creditors, rating agencies, and supervisors

statement: In a robust economic capital framework, the confidence level should not vary according to the constituent perspective.
explanation: Banks explicitly use different confidence levels for different purposes, such as a very high level for solvency and rating targets and lower levels for capital allocation and profit analysis.
originalText: None of the above: in a robust EC framework, confidence level should not vary according to constituent perspective
correction: In a robust economic capital framework, the confidence level can vary according to the constituent perspective.

statement: The variance-covariance approach to risk aggregation depends heavily on correlation pairs that are difficult to estimate, in part because they are time-varying.
explanation: Inter-risk correlations are hard to estimate and may change over time, and the linear structure of the matrix also misses nonlinearities.
originalText: It depends greatly on correlation pairs which are difficult to estimate, in part because they are time‑varying

statement: Operational inter-risk correlations are costly and difficult to estimate because operational loss data are scarce and do not cover long time periods.
explanation: Scarce and short operational loss histories make correlations between operational risk and other risk types hard to estimate, which is a disadvantage of the variance-covariance approach.
originalText: Operational inter‑risk correlations can be costly and difficult to estimate because operational loss ”data are scarce and do not cover long time periods”

statement: By focusing on average covariance between risks, the variance-covariance approach tends to underestimate tail risks.
explanation: Linear, average-based dependence does not capture tail dependence, which is why banks use stressed correlations.
originalText: By focusing on average covariance between risks, the approach will tend to underestimate tail risks

statement: Copulas and full simulation approaches do not necessarily assume linear dependencies between risk types, so they can capture nonlinear dependence.
explanation: Summation, constant diversification and the variance-covariance matrix all assume linear, fixed dependence. Copulas and full simulation of common risk drivers can represent nonlinear dependence.
originalText: Copulas and Simulations

statement: The variance-covariance approach to risk aggregation does not assume linear dependencies between risk types.
explanation: The correlation matrix still assumes linear, time-invariant interactions between risk types, so it cannot capture nonlinear dependence.
originalText: Variance‑covariance
correction: The variance-covariance approach to risk aggregation assumes linear dependencies between risk types.

statement: One of the three supervisory concerns about risk aggregation cited by the BIS is that popular methods are overly dependent on subjective judgment and insufficiently quantitative.
explanation: The BIS concerns are that frameworks are hard to validate, that diversification benefits may be presumed or overestimated, and that sophisticated methods can create false confidence. The BIS accepts that judgment is a necessary complement to quantitative methods.
originalText: Popular methods are overly dependent on subjective judgment and insufficiently quantitative

statement: One supervisory concern about risk aggregation is that popular methodologies, in presuming or over-estimating diversification benefits, may under-estimate true aggregate risk.
explanation: Diversification cannot be taken as given, and mis-measuring it can lead to under-estimating overall risk.
originalText: Popular methodologies, in presuming or over‑estimating diversification benefits, may under‑estimate true aggregate risk

statement: One supervisory concern about risk aggregation is that sophisticated methods, by producing apparently accurate outcomes, may lead to over-confidence or a false sense of confidence.
explanation: Greater sophistication can create unwarranted confidence in the accuracy of aggregate economic capital figures.
originalText: Sophisticated methods, in producing apparently accurate outcomes, may lead to a (behavioral) sense of over‑or false‑confidence

statement: Measuring current exposure is a difficulty in modeling counterparty credit risk in an economic capital framework.
explanation: Current exposure is observable from current mark-to-market values. The genuine difficulties include potential exposure, wrong-way risk and differences between margined and non-margined counterparties.
originalText: Trying to measure current exposure

statement: Measuring potential exposure is a difficulty in modeling counterparty credit risk in an economic capital framework.
explanation: Potential exposure requires simulating risk factors over multiple, long holding periods for the whole portfolio of positions with each counterparty.
originalText: Trying to measure potential exposure

statement: Differences in risk profiles between margined and non-margined counterparties are a difficulty in modeling counterparty credit risk in an economic capital framework.
explanation: Margined counterparties have short forecasting periods and non-margined ones have long periods, and gap risk remains even when positions are margined.
originalText: Differences in risk profiles between margined and non‑margined counterparties

statement: Earnings at risk (EaR) is a main source of interest rate risk in the banking book.
explanation: The main sources are repricing risk, yield curve risk and basis risk. Earnings at risk is a measurement approach that quantifies the loss of net interest income from rate changes, not a source of risk.
originalText: Earnings at risk (EaR)

statement: Repricing risk is a main source of interest rate risk in the banking book.
explanation: Repricing risk arises from differences in the maturity or repricing terms of assets and liabilities. The other main sources are yield curve risk and basis risk.
originalText: Repricing risk

statement: Basis risk is a main source of interest rate risk in the banking book.
explanation: Basis risk arises from the imperfect correlation between the rates earned and paid on instruments with similar repricing characteristics.
originalText: Basis risk

statement: The most conservative estimate of risk is always a simple aggregation of compartmentalized measures.
explanation: Summing separately measured risks is usually conservative, but interactions between risk types can compound so that true integrated risk exceeds the simple sum. For example, FX moves can raise default probabilities on foreign-currency loans.
originalText: The most conservative estimate of risk is always a simple aggregation of compartmentalized measures
correction: The most conservative estimate of risk is not always a simple aggregation of compartmentalized measures.

statement: A compartmentalized approach sums risks measured separately, while a unified approach considers the interaction between these risks explicitly.
explanation: This is the basic contrast the Basel Committee draws between the two approaches to risk measurement.
originalText: A compartmentalized approach sums risks measured separately, while a unified approach considers the interaction between these risks explicitly

statement: From a theoretical perspective, an integrated approach is needed to capture potential compounding effects that are ignored in compartmentalized risk measurement approaches.
explanation: Only an approach that models the interaction between risk types can capture compounding effects, such as foreign-currency loans whose default risk rises when the exchange rate moves against the borrower.
originalText: From a theoretical perspective, an integrated approach is needed to capture potential compounding effects that are ignored in compartmentalized risk measurement approaches

statement: VaR is not subadditive, so the sum of sub-portfolio VaRs can understate the bank-wide VaR.
explanation: Because VaR can violate subadditivity, the bank-wide VaR of a combined portfolio can exceed the sum of the stand-alone VaRs. This causes problems when VaR is used to allocate economic capital and set limits.
originalText: VaR is not subadditive, so the sum of sub‑portfolio VaRs can understate the bank‑wide VaR

statement: VaR violates the monotonicity condition, so a portfolio with higher future returns can show greater risk.
explanation: VaR is monotonic. The monotonicity violation is the criticism of standard deviation, while the main coherence criticism of VaR is that it can violate subadditivity.
originalText: VaR violates monotonicity, so a portfolio with higher future returns can show greater risk

statement: VaR has no clear link to the bank's desired target credit rating.
explanation: VaR is a quantile at a chosen confidence level, which maps directly to a target default probability and hence to a target rating. The lack of a clear link to the target rating is the criticism of expected shortfall.
originalText: VaR has no clear link to the bank’s desired target credit rating

statement: Retail non-maturity deposits are appropriately modeled as floating-rate, putable bonds.
explanation: The bank can reset the deposit rate, which makes the deposit behave like a floating-rate bond, and the depositor can withdraw at par, which is a put option back to the bank.
originalText: The bank models its retail non‑maturity deposits as floating‑rate, putable bonds.

statement: A bank changes the interest rate it offers to depositors by the full amount of any change in market interest rates.
explanation: Banks adjust deposit rates with a lag and by less than the full change in market rates, particularly when rates rise.
originalText: The bank changes the interest rate it offers to depositors by the full amount of any change in market interest rates.
correction: A bank changes the interest rate it offers to depositors by less than the full amount of any change in market interest rates.

changes.to: by less than the full amount of

statement: Residential mortgages exhibit positive convexity as interest rates decrease.
explanation: Mortgages show negative convexity when rates fall because prepayments accelerate, which shortens the life of the cash flows (contraction risk).
originalText: The bank assumes that its residential mortgages exhibit positive convexity as interest rates decrease.
correction: Residential mortgages exhibit negative convexity as interest rates decrease.

statement: Spectral and distorted risk measures are not widely used in practice and are largely of academic interest.
explanation: They are not intuitive, since a spectrum or distortion function must be chosen. VaR and expected shortfall are the most commonly used measures, and standard deviation remains a simple, familiar measure.
originalText: Spectral risk measures.

statement: The copula approach to risk aggregation is characterized by great difficulty in validating the parameterization and in building the joint distribution.
explanation: Copulas are flexible and capture nonlinear and higher-order dependence, but their parameterization is very hard to validate and building the joint distribution is very difficult.
originalText: Copulas.

statement: Benchmarking a model against another model provides little comfort that the model actually reflects reality.
explanation: Benchmarking compares one model or calibration with another, not with actual outcomes, so it only confirms broad comparability and says little about absolute levels or realism.
originalText: Benchmarking.

statement: The BIS recommendation on counterparty credit risk says banks should consider using additional methods, such as stress testing, to help cover all exposures.
explanation: Counterparty credit risk measurement methods involve trade-offs and no single method covers every exposure, so they should be supplemented with complementary methods such as stress testing.
originalText: Counterparty credit risk.

statement: The BIS recommends that all risks should be directly quantified within the economic capital model.
explanation: The BIS acknowledges that not all risks can be directly quantified. Material hard-to-quantify risks, such as funding liquidity and reputational risk, are captured through compensating controls such as sensitivity analysis, stress testing or scenario analysis.
originalText: All risks should be directly quantified within the economic capital model.

statement: A bank should be able to demonstrate how its economic capital model has been integrated into the business decision-making process.
explanation: This follows the BIS recommendation on using internal risk measures to assess capital adequacy: the model must feed real business decisions, not just risk reporting.
originalText: A bank should be able to demonstrate how its economic capital model has been integrated into the business decision‑making process.

statement: Economic capital model validation should be rigorous and comprehensive, aimed at demonstrating that the model is fit for purpose.
explanation: Rigorous and comprehensive validation is one of the BIS recommendations for making effective use of internal risk measures.
originalText: Economic capital model validation should be rigorous and comprehensive, aimed at demonstrating the model is fit for purpose.

statement: An economic capital model helps guide key decisions, such as capital allocation, by assessing the difference between stand-alone and diversified risk.
explanation: The BIS expects the model to be integrated into business decisions, and the board should understand the gap between gross (stand-alone) and net (diversified) risk.
originalText: Our economic capital model helps guide key decisions, such as capital allocation, by assessing the difference between standalone and diversified risk.

statement: A bank should assess whether the dependency structures in its credit portfolio model are appropriate and use supplementary approaches, such as sensitivity and scenario analysis, to address the model's limitations.
explanation: This is the BIS recommendation on dependency modeling in credit risk: scrutinise the dependency structures and cover model limitations with sensitivity and scenario analysis.
originalText: The bank assesses whether the dependency structures in its credit portfolio model are appropriate and uses supplementary approaches such as sensitivity and scenario analysis to address model limitations.

statement: The BIS identifies VaR as the single preferred risk measure for all risk types in economic capital.
explanation: The BIS states that there is no singularly preferred risk measure. Every measure has advantages and disadvantages that must be understood in the context of its intended use.
originalText: The bank adopts VaR as the single preferred risk measure for all risk types, on the basis that BIS identifies it as the best measure for economic capital.

statement: There is no singularly preferred risk measure for economic capital, and a bank should understand the limitations of the measures it uses and the implications of its choice.
explanation: All risk measures have advantages and disadvantages, so the BIS recommendation is to understand them in the context of the intended application rather than to adopt one measure.
originalText: There is no singularly preferred risk measure, and a bank should understand the limitations of the measures it uses and the implications of its choice.

statement: Expected shortfall is free of limitations and should therefore replace VaR as the economic capital risk measure.
explanation: No risk measure is free of limitations. Expected shortfall is hard to interpret and has no clear link to the target rating, and it still needs validation.
originalText: Expected shortfall should replace VaR because it is free of limitations and so needs no further validation.

statement: A loan with higher stand-alone risk always contributes more risk to the portfolio, so ranking loans by stand-alone risk is sufficient to assess concentration.
explanation: Under an economic capital framework, a loan's incremental (marginal) contribution to portfolio risk, not its stand-alone risk, drives the assessment of concentration.
originalText: A loan with higher stand‑alone risk always contributes more risk to the portfolio, so ranking loans by standalone risk is sufficient to assess concentration.

statement: In credit portfolio management under an economic capital framework, the creditworthiness of each borrower is assessed in a portfolio context rather than on a stand-alone basis.
explanation: What matters is how each borrower adds to the risk of the whole portfolio, which depends on concentration and diversification as well as the borrower's own credit quality.
originalText: In credit portfolio management, the creditworthiness of each borrower is assessed in a portfolio context rather than on a stand‑alone basis.

statement: In risk-based pricing, deals whose expected RAROC falls below a given threshold are rejected, so the allocated economic capital sets a floor on the interest rate.
explanation: Allocated economic capital drives a minimum RAROC or a minimum rate that at least does not reduce shareholder value.
originalText: In risk‑based pricing, deals whose expected RAROC falls below a given threshold are rejected, so the allocated economic capital sets a floor on the interest rate.

statement: Linking incentive pay to economic capital does tend to motivate participation in the economic capital allocation process and some such linkage should be attempted, but actual linkage in practice is quite low.
explanation: Incentives are the most sensitive element for most managers, so linkage helps engage them in the allocation process. In practice, compensation schemes rank quite low among the actual uses of economic capital at business-unit level.
originalText: Linking incentive pay to EC DOES tend to motivate participation in the EC allocation process; some such linkage should be attempted, but actual linkage (EC metrics to pay) in practice is quite low

statement: In practice, the linkage of economic capital metrics to pay is already prevalent.
explanation: Compensation schemes rank quite low among the actual uses of economic capital at business-unit level, even though some linkage is encouraged.
originalText: Linking incentive pay to EC DOES tend to motivate participation in the EC allocation process; some such linkage should be attempted, and actual linkage (EC metrics to pay) in practice is already prevalent
correction: In practice, the linkage of economic capital metrics to pay is quite low.

statement: An economic capital framework helps a bank reduce concentration risk by quantifying the incremental risk each loan adds to the total portfolio, which guides rebalancing and hedging decisions.
explanation: A loan's marginal contribution to portfolio risk, rather than its stand-alone risk, shows where concentration lies and which loans to hedge or transfer.
originalText: By quantifying the incremental risk each loan adds to the total portfolio, guiding rebalancing and hedging decisions

statement: Under risk-based pricing, the minimum loan rate covers the cost of funding, expected loss, the cost of the allocated economic capital and the extra return required by shareholders.
explanation: This minimum rate, or equivalently a minimum RAROC, is the floor at which a loan does not reduce shareholder value.
originalText: The minimum rate covers the cost of funding, expected loss, the cost of the allocated economic capital, and the extra return required by shareholders

statement: An economic capital framework supports customer profitability analysis by segmenting customers by net return per unit of risk, which identifies unprofitable customers so that capital can be reallocated to more profitable relationships.
explanation: Economic capital provides the risk base that makes relationship returns comparable per unit of risk, although measuring risk and cost per customer remains difficult.
originalText: By segmenting customers by net return per unit of risk, it identifies unprofitable or marginally profitable customers so capital can be reallocated to more profitable relationships

statement: Of the uses of an economic capital framework, credit portfolio management is the one meant more for protecting against risk deterioration.
explanation: Credit portfolio management uses hedging and risk transfer to control concentration. Risk-based pricing aims at profitability, customer analysis identifies unprofitable customers and management incentives motivate participation.
originalText: Credit portfolio management.

statement: Good governance of an economic capital framework includes formalized change processes and active senior management engagement.
explanation: The reliability of economic capital rests on strong controls over changes to risk measurement techniques, thorough documentation and senior management that is committed to and responsible for the whole process.
originalText: Establishing governance controls, including formalized change processes and active senior management engagement.

statement: Economic capital oversight can be assigned to the finance department with minimal involvement from senior management.
explanation: Senior management must be committed to and responsible for governance of the entire economic capital process and is a main driver of the framework.
originalText: Assigning economic capital oversight to the finance department, with minimal involvement from senior management.

statement: Good governance of an economic capital model requires responsible parties to sign off on methodology changes, diagnostics and formal validation after each change, and internal escalation procedures for unexpectedly large changes in economic capital.
explanation: The reliability of economic capital depends on strong controls over changes, including sign-off, post-change diagnostics and escalation procedures.
originalText: Require responsible parties to sign off on methodology changes, run diagnostics and formal validation after each change, and set internal escalation procedures for unexpectedly large changes in economic capital.

statement: An economic capital model that is used only internally does not need to follow formal change-control processes.
explanation: Being used internally does not remove the need for formal controls, because the reliability of economic capital depends on strong control over changes to the model.
originalText: Allow the economic capital model to be changed at the discretion of the model owner, since the model is used only internally and need not follow change‑control processes.

statement: Economic capital should not be the only measure determining required capital, because banks typically also align capital with target external credit ratings, balancing shareholders' preference for lower capital against rating agencies' preference for higher capital.
explanation: Required capital reflects the tension between shareholders, who want profitability from lower capital, and rating agencies, who encourage solvency through higher capital.
originalText: Economic capital should not be the only measure determining required capital; banks typically also align capital with target external credit ratings, balancing shareholders’ preference for lower capital against rating agencies’ preference for higher capital.

statement: All banks define available capital resources identically.
explanation: There is no common definition of available capital across banks. Most start from Tier 1 capital and adjust it in different ways.
originalText: The proposal is appropriate provided available capital is defined as the standard Tier 1 figure, since all banks define available capital resources identically.

statement: A high-confidence economic capital model makes integrated stress testing unnecessary.
explanation: Integrated stress testing is encouraged to assess the impact of scenarios on economic capital, and a high confidence level does not replace it.
originalText: The proposal is appropriate because a high‑confidence economic capital model makes integrated stress testing unnecessary.

statement: Under the Basel II advanced measurement approach, a bank cannot recognize insurance or other risk mitigants in its operational risk capital calculation.
explanation: The AMA is the approach that allows banks to reflect risk mitigants such as insurance, subject to conditions.
originalText: Under the advanced measurement approach, a bank cannot recognize insurance or other risk mitigants in its capital calculation.
correction: Under the Basel II advanced measurement approach, a bank can recognize insurance or other risk mitigants in its operational risk capital calculation.

statement: Under the Basel II basic indicator approach, operational risk capital is 15% of average annual gross income over the past three years, ignoring years with negative gross income.
explanation: The basic indicator approach applies a single 15% factor to the three-year average of positive annual gross income.
originalText: Under the basic indicator approach, capital is 15% of average annual gross income over the past three years, ignoring years with negative gross income.

statement: Under the Basel II advanced measurement approach, operational risk capital is based on a one-year loss measure at the 99.9% confidence level from the bank's internal model.
explanation: AMA banks estimate a loss distribution from internal models and read the 99.9th percentile over a one-year horizon.
originalText: Under the advanced measurement approach, capital is based on a one‑year operational loss measure at the 99.9% confidence level from internal models.

statement: Basel II was the first bank capital accord to introduce an explicit operational risk capital charge.
explanation: Basel I covered credit risk only, the 1996 Amendment added market risk for the trading book, and Basel II added operational risk with the basic indicator, standardized and advanced measurement approaches.
originalText: Basel II

statement: Basel I required banks to hold capital for operational risk.
explanation: Basel I addressed credit risk only. Operational risk capital was first required under Basel II.
originalText: Basel I
correction: Basel II required banks to hold capital for operational risk.

statement: Two popular approaches to the operational risk advanced measurement approach (AMA) are scenario analysis and the loss distribution approach (parametric and Monte Carlo).
explanation: AMA banks estimate a distribution of operational losses from frequency and severity and read the 99.9th percentile. The loss distribution approach and detailed scenario analysis are the two most widely used methods, and many banks combine them.
originalText: Two popular approaches to the operational risk Advanced Measurement Approach (AMA) are Scenario Analysis and the Loss Distribution Approach (LDA; i.e., parametric and Monte Carlo)

statement: Under Basel II, expected losses are included in the credit risk capital charge but excluded from the operational risk capital charge.
explanation: IRB credit risk capital excludes expected loss, which is covered by loan loss reserves. The AMA operational risk charge is read from the 99.9th percentile of the loss distribution, so expected loss is not excluded there.
originalText: Expected losses are included in the credit risk charge but excluded from the operational risk charge

statement: Under the Basel II internal ratings-based (IRB) approach to credit risk, the default probability (PD) increases as the correlation parameter increases.
explanation: PD is an input to the IRB formula and is not driven by the correlation parameter. In the Basel IRB formula the correlation parameter is itself a decreasing function of PD, and higher correlation raises the worst-case default rate, not PD.
originalText: Under the Internal Ratings Based (IRB) approach to credit risk, default probability (PD) increases as the correlation parameter increases

statement: The operational risk advanced measurement approach (AMA) persisted into Basel III and IV.
explanation: The AMA lost favour because few banks could adopt it successfully, and Basel III replaced it, together with the earlier standardized approaches, with a single standardized approach.
originalText: The operational risk Advanced Measurement Approach (AMA) was one of Basel II’s most successful features such that it persisted into Basel III and IV

statement: A Solvency II internal model must pass a use test, meaning it is genuinely used in business decision making.
explanation: The three internal model tests are statistical quality, calibration and use. The use test requires the model to be embedded in real management decisions.
originalText: Use test.

statement: A Solvency II internal model must pass a calibration test, meaning risks are measured in line with the regulator's SCR target criteria.
explanation: Calibration ties the internal model to the common solvency target set by the regulator rather than to a standard the insurer picks for itself.
originalText: Calibration test.

statement: A Solvency II internal model must be used in actual business decision making, not just for regulatory reporting.
explanation: This is the use test: the model must be embedded in real management decisions rather than being merely a compliance exercise.
originalText: The model must be used in actual business decision making, not just for regulatory reporting.

statement: Under Solvency II, risks in an internal model must be calibrated to a target standard chosen by the insurer rather than by the regulator.
explanation: Calibration is to the regulator's SCR target criteria, which give a common standard across insurers.
originalText: Risks must be calibrated to a target standard chosen by the insurer rather than the regulator.
correction: Under Solvency II, risks in an internal model must be calibrated to a target standard chosen by the regulator rather than by the insurer.

changes.from: chosen by the insurer rather than by the regulator
changes.to: chosen by the regulator rather than by the insurer

statement: A Solvency II internal model must be based on a 99.9% confidence level over a one-year horizon.
explanation: Solvency II uses a one-year VaR at the 99.5% confidence level. The 99.9% level is the Basel II credit and operational risk level.
originalText: The model must be based on a 99.9% confidence level over a one‑year horizon.
correction: A Solvency II internal model must be based on a 99.5% confidence level over a one-year horizon.

statement: Similar to Basel II, Solvency II has three pillars and three tiers of capital.
explanation: Solvency II's pillars cover quantitative requirements, governance and supervision, and disclosure. Its capital is divided into Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3.

statement: Similar to Basel II, Solvency II is an international regulatory standard.
explanation: Solvency II is a European Union regime for insurers, not an international standard.

statement: Solvency II considers three risks: credit, market and operational risk.
explanation: Solvency II also charges for underwriting risk, which is the key insurer-specific risk. Its charges cover underwriting, investment (market and credit) and operational risk.
originalText: Similar to Basel II, Solvency II considers three risks: credit, market and operational risk.

statement: If capital drops below the Solvency II minimum capital requirement (MCR), supervisors are likely to insist that the insurer add new business and underwrite additional policies to increase earned premiums.
explanation: A breach of the MCR leads supervisors to restrict new business or to resolve the firm, for example through sale or liquidation, not to encourage more underwriting.
originalText: If capital drops below the MCR level, supervisors are likely to insist that the insurance company add new businesses and underwrite additional policies to increase earned premiums.

statement: If capital drops below the Solvency II solvency capital requirement (SCR), the insurer should, at minimum, deliver to the supervisor a plan to restore capital to above the SCR.
explanation: A breach of the SCR calls for a capital restoration plan, and the supervisor may impose additional measures.
originalText: If capital drops below the SCR level, an insurance company should, at minimum, deliver to the supervisor a plan to restore capital to above the SCR level.

statement: If capital drops below the Solvency II minimum capital requirement (MCR), supervisors might force the insurer into liquidation and the transfer of its policies to another company.
explanation: The MCR is the absolute floor, and breaching it can lead to a ban on new policies or to resolution through sale or liquidation.
originalText: If capital drops below the MCR level, supervisors might force the insurance company into liquidation, transferring its policies to another company.

statement: Under the Solvency II internal models approach, the SCR is based on a one-year VaR at the 99.5% confidence level, lower than the 99.9% level used for credit and operational risk under Basel II.
explanation: Solvency II uses a one-year 99.5% VaR, while Basel II uses a one-year 99.9% level for credit and operational risk.
originalText: The internal models approach uses a VaR with a one‑year horizon and a 99.5% confidence level, lower than the 99.9% level used for credit and operational risk under Basel II.

statement: Under Solvency II, all qualifying capital must be Tier 1 capital.
explanation: Solvency II capital has three tiers, and requirements may be met by a combination of Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 capital. Tier 1 is equity-type capital, while liabilities subordinated to policyholders fall in Tier 2 or Tier 3.
originalText: All qualifying capital must be Tier 1, which can consist only of liabilities that are subordinated to policyholders and satisfy availability criteria in wind‑down scenarios.

statement: Under Solvency II, capital requirements may be met by a combination of Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 capital, as under Basel II.
explanation: Tier 1 is equity and retained earnings, Tier 2 is subordinated liabilities available in liquidation, and Tier 3 is subordinated capital that does not meet other criteria.
originalText: Capital requirements may be met by a combination of Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 capital, similar to Basel II.

statement: Reputational risk carries a specific capital charge in the Solvency II solvency capital requirement (SCR).
explanation: The SCR has charges for underwriting risk (life, non-life and health), investment risk (market and credit) and operational risk. Reputational risk has no separate charge.
originalText: Reputational risk.

statement: Underwriting risk carries a specific capital charge in the Solvency II solvency capital requirement (SCR).
explanation: Underwriting risk is the insurer-specific charge and is subdivided into life, non-life and health.
originalText: Underwriting risk.

statement: Investment risk, both market and credit, carries a specific capital charge in the Solvency II solvency capital requirement (SCR).
explanation: Investment risk has its own SCR charge, subdivided into market risk and credit risk.
originalText: Investment (market and credit) risk.

statement: Solvency II specifies both a solvency capital requirement (SCR) and a minimum capital requirement (MCR).
explanation: The MCR is the absolute floor and the SCR is set above it, so the gap between them acts as a buffer.
originalText: It specifies both a solvency capital requirement (SCR) and a minimum capital requirement (MCR).

statement: Solvency II requires a single minimum ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets and allows no internal models.
explanation: Solvency II allows insurers to compute the SCR with an internal model as well as the standardized approach, and it is not a risk-weighted-assets ratio.
originalText: It requires a single minimum ratio of capital to risk‑weighted assets, with no internal models allowed.

statement: The Solvency II internal models approach to the SCR is similar to the Basel II internal ratings-based approach in that the firm must calculate a VaR with a one-year time horizon.
explanation: Both rest on a one-year horizon, although the confidence level differs: 99.5% under Solvency II and 99.9% under Basel II.
originalText: The internal models approach to calculating the solvency capital requirement is similar to internal ratings‑based approach under Basel II in that the firm must calculate a VaR with a one‑year time horizon.

statement: The minimum capital requirement is higher than the solvency capital requirement for insurance companies.
explanation: The MCR is the absolute floor and lies below the SCR, so the SCR is the higher requirement.
originalText: The minimum capital requirement is likely to be higher than the solvency capital requirement for insurance companies.
correction: The minimum capital requirement is lower than the solvency capital requirement for insurance companies.

statement: The repercussion for violating the solvency capital requirement is likely liquidation and the transfer of the company's insurance policies to another firm.
explanation: Liquidation or transfer of policies is a consequence of breaching the MCR. Breaching the SCR calls for a capital restoration plan and possible supervisory measures.
originalText: The repercussion for violating the solvency capital requirement is likely liquidation and the transfer of company insurance policies to another firm.

statement: The Volcker Rule generally prohibits proprietary trading at firms that take insured deposits.
explanation: The Volcker Rule restricts proprietary trading and investment in hedge funds and private equity at deposit-taking firms, because banks funded by insured deposits should not speculate with their own capital.
originalText: The Volcker Rule would generally prohibit the desk because it restricts proprietary trading at deposit‑taking firms.

statement: A standardized over-the-counter interest rate swap between two financial institutions may be traded on a swap execution facility and must be cleared through a central counterparty.
explanation: Post-crisis reforms moved standardized OTC derivatives onto swap execution facilities, which promote price transparency, and required derivatives between financial institutions to be centrally cleared.
originalText: The swap may be traded on a swap execution facility and must be cleared through a central counterparty.

statement: Under the Basel standardized approach, operational risk capital is the Business Indicator multiplied by marginal coefficients of 12%, 15% and 18% and scaled by the Internal Loss Multiplier, where the Business Indicator is built from income statement and balance sheet items.
explanation: The Business Indicator Component applies 12% up to EUR 1 billion, 15% from EUR 1 billion to 30 billion and 18% above EUR 30 billion, and capital equals the BIC multiplied by the Internal Loss Multiplier.
originalText: The ORC is a percentage (i.e., 12\|15\|18% marginal coefficient) of the Business Indicator (BI) scaled by the Internal Loss Multiplier (ILM), where the BI is the sum of various income statement and/or balance sheet items

statement: Under the Basel standardized approach, operational risk capital is the minimum of 2.25% of interest-earning assets and the absolute value of net interest income.
explanation: That minimum is only the cap on the net interest term inside the interest, lease and dividend component of the Business Indicator. Capital is the Business Indicator Component multiplied by the Internal Loss Multiplier.
originalText: The ORC is the minimum of either (i) 2.25% of interest‑earning assets or (ii) the absolute value of the net interest income

statement: Under the Basel standardized approach, operational risk capital is a 12, 15 or 18 times multiple of the average annual losses incurred over the previous ten years.
explanation: Losses enter only through the loss component of the Internal Loss Multiplier, which uses 15 times average annual loss over ten years. The 12%, 15% and 18% coefficients apply to the Business Indicator.
originalText: The ORC is a multiple (i.e., 12x\|15x\|18x scalar multiplier) of the average annual losses incurred over the ten previous years

statement: Under the Basel III standardized approach, a bank with a Business Indicator above EUR 1 billion must incorporate its own loss experience in the operational risk capital calculation.
explanation: Banks with a Business Indicator above EUR 1 billion fall in bucket 2 or higher and use their own loss data through the Internal Loss Multiplier. Banks in bucket 1 have an ILM of 1.
originalText: Bank B would be expected to use loss experience in the standardized approach calculations.

statement: The Business Indicator includes an administrative component covering insurance premiums paid or received, changes in goodwill and the maximum of staff expenses or outsourcing fees.
explanation: The Business Indicator has exactly three components: the interest, leases and dividend component, the services component and the financial component. Administrative expenses are excluded.
originalText: The administrative component (AC) includes insurance premiums paid/received, recognized changes in goodwill, and the maximum of (staff expenses; or outsourcing fees)

statement: The financial component of the Business Indicator includes the net profit or loss on the trading book and the banking book.
explanation: The financial component is the absolute value of net trading book P&L plus the absolute value of net banking book P&L, each averaged over three years.
originalText: The financial component (FC) includes net profit/loss on the trading and banking books

statement: The interest, leases and dividend component of the Business Indicator adds average dividend income to the minimum of average net interest income and a percentage of interest-earning assets.
explanation: Net interest income is capped at 2.25% of interest-earning assets, and dividend income is then added.
originalText: The interest, leases, and dividend component (ILDC) adds average dividend income to the minimum of (average net interest income; or a percentage of interest‑earning assets)

statement: A bank first moving to the Basel III standardized approach for operational risk can use the loss component if it has at least five years of good-quality, reliable loss data.
explanation: Ideally the loss component uses ten years of high-quality annual loss data, but as a transition a minimum of five years is allowed. The age of the bank is not the test.
originalText: Yes, as the bank will be eligible as long as the loss data covering at least the last 5 years is deemed good quality and reliable.

statement: The financial component of the Business Indicator takes into account a bank's trading book and banking book P&L results.
explanation: The financial component is the absolute value of net trading book P&L plus the absolute value of net banking book P&L.
originalText: Financial component.

statement: The loss component is part of the Business Indicator calculation.
explanation: The loss component is not part of the Business Indicator. It feeds the Internal Loss Multiplier and reflects the bank's internal operational losses.
originalText: Loss component.

statement: Provisions and reversals of provisions related to operational loss events are included in the Business Indicator.
explanation: Provisions and their reversals are excluded from the Business Indicator unless they relate to operational loss events, in which case they are captured in other operating income or expenses.
originalText: Provision reversals related to operational loss events.

statement: Administrative expenses, including staff and outsourcing costs, are included in the Business Indicator.
explanation: Administrative expenses, insurance premiums paid and depreciation of tangible and intangible assets are excluded from the Business Indicator.
originalText: Administrative expenses.
